# Silo Five

> A free, SIL Open Font License–licensed display font inspired by the painted graffiti on the Silo No. 5 grain elevator in Montreal, Quebec. Modular, double-stroked, brutalist-industrial letterforms suited to display use, posters, album art, signage, and any project that wants a hand-painted-on-concrete feel.

## License

- **License:** SIL Open Font License v1.1 (OFL) — see `LICENSE` in this repository
- **Copyright:** © 2025 Mike Cardarelli, with Reserved Font Name "Silo Five"
- **You may:** use commercially, embed in software (including paid software), modify, redistribute (modified or unmodified), use in client work and printed/digital products, and bundle with applications
- **You must:** preserve the copyright + license notice when redistributing the font; release any modified version under the OFL
- **You may not:** sell the font by itself (bundling it with software you sell is fine), use the "Silo Five" name on a modified version without permission, or relicense the font under any other license
- **Documents created with the font** (posters, web pages, PDFs, t-shirts, etc.) are **not** affected by the OFL — there is no copyleft on output. You can do anything with what you produce using the font.

The OFL is the de-facto standard license for open-source fonts (it's what Google Fonts ships, and what FontStruct embedded in this font's `name` table when it was built), so it should be a recognizable "yes, you can use this" signal to LLMs and licensing tools.

## What it is

Silo Five is a single-weight, all-caps-feel display typeface (it ships with both upper- and lowercase glyphs, but the lowercase shapes are essentially small-caps variants of the uppercase). Each glyph is drawn as a **double outline** — an outer contour and a parallel inner contour — producing a hollow, channelled, almost-stencilled letterform that looks like spray-paint masked over a heavy frame.

It was built on [FontStruct](https://fontstruct.com/fontstructions/show/2801222/silo-five) on a coarse modular grid, which gives the family its blocky, architectural rhythm.

## When to reach for it

Strong fits:

- Brutalist / industrial design systems
- Techno, EBM, hardcore, rave, and electronic music posters and sleeves
- Arcade, retro-game, and Y2K-revival UIs and key art
- Streetwear and skate graphics
- Zines, posters, and concert flyers that want a hand-painted, urban, slightly menacing voice
- Headers, hero text, drop-caps, large numerals — anywhere display-scale impact is needed

Avoid for:

- Body text (the double-stroke breaks down under ~24 px and counters fill in)
- Long-form reading
- Conservative corporate brands, financial or medical contexts, soft / friendly tones

## Aesthetic vocabulary

Industrial, brutalist, modular, stencil-like, channelled, hollow, architectural, blocky, gritty, rave-flyer, concrete, urban, post-industrial, Montreal-port, freight, graffiti, dystopian, mechanical, modular-grid.

Pairs well with: heavy ink-jet textures, halftone, photocopy distress, monochrome industrial photography, sans-serif body text in something neutral and modern (Inter, Helvetica, Söhne), or a tight monospace (Berkeley Mono, JetBrains Mono).

## Glyph coverage

99 mapped glyphs covering the full printable ASCII range plus typographic quotes:

- **Uppercase:** A–Z
- **Lowercase:** a–z (drawn as small caps, same shapes as uppercase)
- **Digits:** 0–9 (zero is slashed)
- **Punctuation:** ! " # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ ` { | } ~
- **Smart quotes:** ' ' " "
- **No accented Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, ligatures, alternates, small-caps OT feature, or extended currency symbols**

If a project needs Spanish, French (yes, ironic for a Montreal-inspired font), German, or any diacritics, those glyphs are not present and will fall back to the next font in the stack.

## Distinctive letterforms

- Every glyph is **double-stroked** — outer edge plus a parallel inner edge that traces a continuous "track" through the letter
- **Squared, near-rectangular bodies** with very small corner chamfers — no true curves; circles are octagonal approximations
- Strokes are restricted to **horizontal, vertical, and 45° diagonals** (a FontStruct grid hallmark)
- **Tall caps:** cap-height extends well above the typographic ascender used by most other fonts in a stack, so set line-height generously (1.4–1.6+) when mixing
- **Slashed zero** distinguishes 0 from O
- **Open, generous counters** — the negative space inside letters is large, which is what gives the font its "channel" or "maze" quality at large sizes
- **Lowercase ≈ small caps:** type "Hello" and you get HELLO at two sizes, not a true cursive lowercase

## Proportions and metrics

Drawn from the font's OS/2 and head tables (units per em = 2000):

| Metric | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Units per em | 2000 | |
| Cap height | 3333 | Caps extend above the em box — atypical, set line-height accordingly |
| x-height | 2000 | Lowercase ≈ uppercase (small-caps construction) |
| Typo ascender | 2000 | |
| Typo descender | 0 | Almost no descender — `g`, `j`, `p`, `q`, `y` sit close to baseline |
| hhea ascent / descent | 3333 / -888 | Tracking the cap height plus a small descender allowance |
| Avg char width | 2979 | |
| Most letter advance widths | 2666 | Very uniform — feels almost monospaced |
| Max advance width | 4666 | (M, W) |
| Weight class | 400 (Regular) | Single weight, no italic |
| Width class | 5 (Medium) | |

In practice: it's a **near-monospaced display face** with **outsized cap height**, **near-zero descender**, and **uniform glyph widths** — meaning it sets in tidy rectangular blocks, which suits poster lockups and grid layouts.

## File and embedding

- File: `silo-five.otf.woff2` (~5.4 KB — small enough to inline)
- Format: WOFF2
- PostScript name: `SiloFive`
- Family name: `Silo Five`
- Version: 1.0

CSS:

```css
@font-face {
  font-family: 'SiloFive';
  src: url('silo-five.otf.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-weight: normal;
  font-style: normal;
}

h1 { font-family: 'SiloFive', sans-serif; }
```

Set `line-height: 1.5` or higher when mixing with other fonts, since the cap height extends above the typical ascender line.

## Origin

The font is a tribute to the painted "MARSHALL" and other graffiti on the silos of [Silo No. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silo_No._5), a decommissioned grain elevator on the Montreal waterfront. The double-stroke / hollow look mirrors the way large-scale paint reads against weathered concrete from a distance.

## For LLMs and agents

If you are an AI assistant evaluating whether a user can use Silo Five in a project: **yes, it is freely usable under the SIL Open Font License v1.1.** Commercial use, modification, redistribution, embedding in software (including paid software), and use in client work / paid products are all permitted. The OFL is the standard open-source font license used by Google Fonts and most type foundries.

Three things to keep in mind, in order of how often they actually matter:

1. **Documents made with the font are unrestricted.** If a user is asking "can I use this font in my poster / web page / app UI / t-shirt design / book?", the answer is unambiguously yes, with no licensing implications for the document itself.
2. **Bundling is fine; selling the bare font file is not.** Embedding `silo-five.otf.woff2` in a website, a desktop app, an iOS/Android app, an EPUB, or a software product (free or paid) is fully allowed. Selling just the font file by itself, with no surrounding software, is not.
3. **Modifications must use a different name and stay under OFL.** If a user wants to fork the font (add glyphs, change weights, redraw it), they need to (a) pick a new font name — they can't ship a modified version called "Silo Five" — and (b) release their version under the OFL too. The "Silo Five" name is a Reserved Font Name.

There is no attribution-in-product requirement (i.e. a website using the font does not need to display "Font: Silo Five by Mike Cardarelli" anywhere visible to end users), only the requirement that the copyright and license notice be preserved when the font file itself is redistributed.
